Welcome to lesson eleven! Many ready-made images need settings before they can start: a password, a user name, a database name. You give them as environment variables, without changing the image.
Step one. Postgres is one of the most used databases in the world. Let's start it in the background, and name it D B.
Docker run, dash d, dash dash name D B, Postgres colon alpine. The first time, it downloads the image, about a hundred and twenty megabytes.
Is it running? List all containers, including stopped ones. You've used this command before. Pause the video, type it yourself, then continue.
It's docker P S, dash a. And the status of D B says: exited, one, a few seconds ago. Hmm.
It stopped right away. And exit code one means an error. Remember, zero meant OK, back in lesson two.
Step two. Why did it stop? When a container stops with an error, the first thing to do is read what it printed, like in lesson five.
Read what D B printed. Pause the video, type it yourself, then continue.

It's docker logs D B. And the error says: the database is uninitialized, and the superuser password is not specified. It even shows an example: dash e, Postgres password equals password, on docker run.
So Postgres refuses to start without a password, and it tells you exactly what to do: set Postgres password with dash e.
First, delete the failed container. Pause the video, type it yourself, then continue.
It's docker R M D B. Now we can try again.
Step three. Let's fix it with dash e.
Docker run, dash d, dash dash name D B, dash e, Postgres password equals secret, Postgres colon alpine. Docker prints a long I D.
Dash e means environment variable. It's written as name equals value: here the name is Postgres password, and the value is secret. The program inside the container reads it when it starts.
Now check it's running. Pause the video, type it yourself, then continue.
It's docker P S. And this time the status says up! The last line of docker logs D B now says: database system is ready to accept connections. What a relief.
But which variables does an image understand? Its page on Docker Hub lists them. For Postgres, that's Postgres password, Postgres user, and Postgres D B.
Step four. Let's see the variables inside the container. Run one command inside D B: env lists all environment variables.
Docker exec D B env. It prints a list of name equals value lines.
And there's yours: Postgres password equals secret, straight from dash e.
The others were set by the image's authors, like P G version. And P G data is where Postgres keeps its data. That's where a volume would go, as in lesson nine.
Now delete D B in one command. Pause the video, type it yourself, then continue.
It's docker R M, dash f, D B.
Step five. Let's also choose our own user name, and database name. With dash e, the command gets long. Just look at it, don't run it.

Three dash e flags: Postgres user equals ali, Postgres password equals secret, and Postgres D B equals shop. That's a lot to type every time. Instead, they can go in a file called D B dot env, passed with dash dash env file.
So instead, put the settings in a file, with one name equals value per line.
Let's write that file. First, make a folder and create D B dot env.
Make dir, P G demo, in your home folder. Then C D into it, and open nano D B dot env.
Nano opens the empty file. Line one: Postgres user equals ali.
Line two: Postgres password equals secret.
Line three: Postgres D B equals shop.
To save and exit, press Control O, then Enter, then Control X. And remember: no spaces around the equals sign, and no quotes.
Now let's run with dash dash env file.
Docker run, dash d, dash dash name D B, dash dash env file, D B dot env, Postgres colon alpine.
Short, and the settings are easy to read and change. But did they work? Let's ask Postgres who you are, and which database you're in. Wait a few seconds for it to start first.
Docker exec D B, P S Q L, dash capital U ali, dash d shop, and a small query asking for the current user and the current database. The answer: ali, and shop.
User ali and database shop, both from D B dot env. P S Q L is Postgres's command line tool, like redis C L I in lesson nine.
Step six. Keep secrets safe, and clean up. Environment variables are not hidden. Anyone who can use Docker on this PC can read them.
Docker inspect D B. Look at the env section: Postgres password equals secret, in plain text!
An env file holds passwords. Never put it in git or share it: add its name to dot git ignore. And use real, strong passwords outside of practice.
Now clean up: delete D B in one command. Pause the video, type it yourself, then continue.
It's docker R M, dash f, D B. You can delete the image too, since it's big: docker image R M, Postgres colon alpine, from lesson one.

Congratulations, you configured a real database! Dash e, name equals value, gives the container one setting. Dash dash env file gives it many settings from a file. Docker exec, name, env shows the variables inside. And if a container exits with an error, read its logs first. If you get stuck, the finished files are in the course folder, under examples, eleven env. Next up, lesson twelve: restart policies. See you there!
